children: Stock index futures were little changed on Tuesday as President Donald Trump raised the prospect of a negotiated end to the U.S. conflict with Iran.
Here are the five news items investors should watch:
Anthropic weighs 1 GW data center deal:
Anthropic is in early discussions to lease as much as 1 gigawatt of computing
from Stream Data Centers, according to The Information. The facilities, majority-owned by Apollo Global Management
, could use AI accelerators from Broadcom
and Alphabet (GOOG, GOOGL), with Nvidia
chips also under consideration. The potential deal highlights continued demand for large-scale AI infrastructure.
Trump reports $270M of July securities trades:
President Donald Trump disclosed 1,156 securities transactions in July, with a combined reported value ranging from roughly $79M to $270M. The portfolio sold at least $35.6M of securities,
Microsoft
and Amazon
, while purchases totaled at least $43.6M. The disclosure provides fresh visibility into the president's reported market activity.
Burry adds to semiconductor and AI shorts:
Michael Burry said he increased short positions in Micron
, Nebius
, the iShares Semiconductor ETF
, and Palantir
, describing the additions as
made “in some size.” He also added to QXO
, Build-A-Bear Workshop
, Sprouts Farmers Market
, Birkenstock
, and MercadoLibre
, calling the latter five full positions.
Alibaba expands European, Middle East data centers:
Alibaba

is accelerating data center development across Europe and the Middle East as it works toward a 20-gigawatt global infrastructure buildout, according to Bloomberg and the South China Morning Post. Alibaba Cloud plans new regions in Turkey, Finland, and the Netherlands over the next year, with the Netherlands facility expected to open in October. The expansion adds to competition for global AI infrastructure capacity.
New customs rule could hit Canadian drug imports:

Prescription medications mailed into the U.S. from abroad will face a customs process requiring a licensed broker and financial guarantee starting Oct. 22. The change follows the broader suspension of the $800 de minimis exemption for imports and could affect Americans who rely on lower-cost mail-order medications from Canada and other countries. The rule may increase costs and logistical requirements for cross-border pharmacy shipments.
